title: Mastering Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) & Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, pathophysiology, and management of Tractional Retinal Detachment, specifically in the context of advanced Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) with vitreous hemorrhage.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) is the second most common type of retinal detachment. It occurs when neurosensory retina is pulled away from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) by contracting vitreoretinal membranes. Unlike Rhegmatogenous RD, TRD is typically associated with a concave surface and lacks a causative retinal break in its pure form.

sections.title: Etiology: Causes of TRD in Both Eyes
Pathophysiology: The Ischemic Cascade
content: Step 1: Capillary non-perfusion leads to chronic retinal ischemia.
Step 2: Upregulation of Pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF, bFGF).
Step 3: Neovascularization (NVD/NVE) grows along the posterior hyaloid face.
Step 4: Fibroglial proliferation accompanies the vessels, forming contractile membranes.
Step 5: Vitreous contraction exerts tangential and anteroposterior traction on the retina.
Step 6: Progressive elevation of the retina (TRD) ± Vitreous Hemorrhage from fragile vessels.

sections.title: Symptomatology & Features
content: Painless, progressive visual field loss.
Sudden vision drop if Vitreous Hemorrhage occurs.
Photopsia (flashing lights) is less common than in RRD.
Metamorphopsia if the macula is distorted by tractional bands.
History of poorly controlled Diabetes Mellitus or prior laser treatment.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Imaging & Exams
content: B-Scan Ultrasonography: Essential if media is opaque (VH). Shows 'tenting' or 'table-top' configuration.
Wide-field Fundus Photography (Optos): To document PRP status and NVE locations.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Assess for Macular Edema or subclinical macular detachment.
Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Identify areas of active leakage (NVD/NVE) and ischemia.
Gonioscopy: To rule out Neovascularization of the Angle (NVA).

sections.title: Management: The Affected Eye (TRD + VH)
content: Step 1: Pre-operative Anti-VEGF (e.g., Bevacizumab) 3-7 days prior to surgery to reduce intraoperative bleeding.
Step 2: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) - 23, 25, or 27 Gauge.
Step 3: Core Vitrectomy and induction of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (if not present).
Step 4: Membrane Peeling: Segmentation (cutting bridges) and Delamination (stripping membranes from retinal surface).
Step 5: Control of Hemorrhage using endodiathermy or increasing infusion pressure.
Step 6: Completion of Panretinal Photocoagulation (Endolaser) to all ischemic peripheral retina.
Step 7: Internal Tamponade (Air, Gas, or Silicone Oil) if iatrogenic breaks or significant traction remain.

sections.title: Management: The Fellow Eye (Post-PRP)
content: Monitor for 'PRP Creep' or regression of NVE.
Supplementary PRP (Fill-in laser) if new NVE or NVD appears.
Anti-VEGF injections if Center-Involving Diabetic Macular Edema (CI-DME) is present.
Strict Glycemic and Blood Pressure control (HbA1c target <7.0%).
Regular follow-up every 3-4 months depending on stability.

sections.title: Red Flags: Surgical Emergencies
content: Macula-threatening TRD (Rapidly progressing towards the fovea).
Combined Tractional-Rhegmatogenous RD (TRRD) - requires urgent repair.
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) with elevated IOP.
Dense Vitreous Hemorrhage obscuring retinal view for >1 month.
Sudden 'Crunch Syndrome' (rapid TRD progression) after Anti-VEGF injection.

content.explanation: V: Vitreous Hemorrhage; I: Ischemia; T: Tractional RD; R: Rubeosis Iridis; E: Edema (Macular); O: Oil/Gas Tamponade; U: Upregulated VEGF; S: Segmentation/Delamination.

rows: PRP reduces the risk of severe vision loss by >50% in high-risk PDR.
Defined 'High-Risk PDR' and timing for laser intervention.
Ranibizumab is non-inferior to PRP for proliferative disease over 2 years.
Vitrectomy vs. Anti-VEGF for VH: Similar visual outcomes at 2 years; surgery faster for recovery.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Resident Tips
content: Always check for NVI before dilating a patient with dense VH.
In TRD, the 'peak' of the tent is usually the site of strongest vitreoretinal adhesion.
Avoid giving Anti-VEGF too early (e.g., >10 days before surgery) in eyes with severe traction to prevent 'The Crunch'.
B-scan 'V' shape: If the apex is at the disc, suspect TRD; if the apex is at the optic nerve head but mobile, suspect PVD.
Endolaser should be applied 360 degrees to the periphery, not just the area of detachment.
